translation:
But when, having vowed that he would burn him, he arrived on the earth, Ambarish became overjoyed. Shyamdas says: praising him again and again, he ran and fell at his feet.

It is said in Bhagwat, Skandha 9, Chapter 4, verses 18 to 21, that King Ambarish kept his mind fixed on the lotus feet of the Lord, sang His praises with his speech, kept his hands engaged in service, listened to Hari's stories with his ears, and gazed upon Hari's image with his eyes — thus he kept all his limbs engaged in devotion to the Lord. In this way Durvasa too sang the glory of devotees. Here is a pada by Agradasji that further extols this glory.

Raag Dhanashri:

_karahu kaun barad ki laaj._
_ab jaanahu pratigya hit ki re, nirno nibedo aaj._ ||karahu||
_aaratvant dvij jan mein hun hari, itno barad sambharyo._
_saachi kahu suno durvasa, meri shakti satantar naahi._
_mere bhakt aadhin sadaai, jaise kit panjra maanhi._ ||karahu|| ||3||
_mukh kijiye ki jaane pari harijana meru manko bhor._
_agradas swami tinsu saar grahi mohe or._ ||karahu|| ||4||

(Whose vow's honour will you now keep? Now understand that the resolve of true devotion must today, once for all, be settled. I, Hari, have kept in mind only this one vow — to be present for the afflicted twice-born. Hear the truth, O Durvasa: my power is not independent — my devotees always hold it in their control, as a bird held within a cage. Whether I should speak of it or not, my devotees know the innermost turn of my mind, like the dawn; Swami Agradas has grasped the essence of these and holds only to that.)

Meaning: Agradasji has sung that the Lord's own vow was that, however great a sinner may come to His refuge, He grants him freedom from fear. And His other vow is that the Lord is ever tender toward His devotees (bhakt-vatsal). Now, of these two vows, which one will the Lord keep? It will now become clear which vow He upholds — the well-being of the one who has taken refuge, or the well-being of His devotee — and today, on this very occasion, that will be decided. The Lord says: "O afflicted Brahmin, the one vow I shall keep today is only this — that I am the one who shows grace to My devotee. I have decided, after due thought, that I will look only to My bond with My devotee. O Durvasa! If you wish to hear more from Me, listen: the divine power that is in Me is not an independent power of Mine — it is always subordinate to My devotee. Just as a parrot shut in a cage is not free, so too am I dependent upon My devotee. Now keep this word of Mine fixed in your heart — that devotees, in My own mind, are like the dawn that gives Me light." For Agradas's worshipped Lord, all the rest of the Lord's other vows fall away before this one — that is, no other vow of the Lord stands before the glory of His being ever-tender to His devotees.

Like Agradas, Kabirji too composed two padas concerning Durvasa and Ambarish; since these are Kabir's own compositions, we ought to give them our attention.

Velaval:

_bhai re kamalnayan prabhu keshava suno tribhuvannath._
_tera jan hoi kyun dare, jaake mastak haatha._ ||tek||
_jal pesat jokham bhayo, kunjar dukh paayo._
_tab raghunath pokariya, tatkaal chhodaayo._ ||kamal|| ||1||
_jal thal giri jwaala thaki, prahlaad ugaaryo._
_narsinh hoy ke pragate, hiranyakashipu maaryo._ ||kamal|| ||2||
_amaresh kere kaarane, (hariliya) dhariya avataara._
_naamdev kirtan kari, hariye pheryo dwaara._ ||kamal|| ||3||
_bhai re paravati rang raachiya, mahadev ugarya._
_lei kankan kar sir dharya, bhasam hokar jaalya._ ||kamal|| ||4||
_charane ahalya uddhari draupadi pat raakhi._
_kahet kabir saanso keso, jaaki nigam he saakhi._ ||5||

(O brother, listen: Keshava, lord of the three worlds, has eyes like the lotus — why should he who becomes His devotee, whose head rests beneath His own hand, ever fear? When the elephant, falling into deep water, fell into distress and cried out in pain, he cried out to Raghunath, who came and freed him at once. From water, land, mountain and fire the Lord saved Prahlad, and appearing in the form of Narasimha, killed Hiranyakashipu. For the sake of Ambarish He took incarnations; because Namdev performed kirtan, Hari turned the temple's very door around for him. O brother, even Mahadev, absorbed in delight with Parvati, was saved — he placed a bangled hand upon his own head and was burnt to ash. By whose feet Ahalya was redeemed and Draupadi's honour was preserved — Kabir says, why keep any doubt about such a One, for whom even the Vedas themselves stand as witness?)

Meaning: O brother, listen — Keshava, the lord of the three worlds, whose eyes are like the lotus, why should one who becomes His devotee, upon whose head His own hand rests, hold any fear? When the elephant fell into the water and, caught in that trouble, suffered greatly, it called out to Ram, who at once rescued it. From water, from land, from mountain, and from fire He saved Prahlad, and appearing in the form of Narasimha, He slew Hiranyakashipu. For Ambarish's sake He took ten incarnations. Namdev performed devotion and did a wonderful deed through it; the Lord turned round the very door of the temple. O brother, even Mahadev, who delights in play with Parvati, was likewise saved — he was made to place a bangled hand upon his own head, and by that Bhasmasur was burnt to ashes. By whose feet Ahalya was redeemed, and Draupadi's honour preserved — for this, says Kabirji, even the Vedas stand as testimony, so why should we harbour any doubt? Here is a second pada, also by Kabirji.

Godi:

_man re tu hari bhaj bhai (-2)_
_ja din tera koi na hosi, ta din raam sahaai._ ||tek||
_tantra na jaanu mantra na jaanu, na jaanu sundar kaaya._
_mir malak bade raaja raana, te sab khaaye maayaa._ ||1||
_ved na jaanu bhed na jaanu, jaanu ek hi raama._
_panditkun pachhwaada kina, dwaar kiyo jit naama._ ||2||
_raaja amareeshke sukh kaaran, chakra sudarshan jaaryo._
_daas kabirko eso thaakor, bhagatke sharan ubaaro._ ||3||

(O mind, worship Hari, O brother — worship Hari! The day when no one will be yours, on that day Ram alone will be your help. I know no tantra, I know no mantra, I do not even understand the beauty of the body — for maya devours even the great chiefs, kings, and rulers of a kingdom. I know no Vedas, I know no secret doctrine, I know only the one Ram. He set the pundits behind, and turned the temple's door to face where Namdev stood. For King Ambarish's happiness and welfare, He hurled the Sudarshan chakra. Such, says the servant Kabir, is my mighty Lord, who saves the devotee who has taken His refuge.)

Meaning: O mind, worship Hari — for the day when you have no one else, Ram alone will help you then. I know neither tantra nor mantra, nor do I even understand bodily beauty, for maya devours even the great chiefs, rulers, and kings of a realm. I know neither the Vedas nor their secret meaning; I know only the one Ram. He set the Brahmin pundits behind the temple and turned its main door to face the direction where Namdev stood. To bring happiness (that is, to save) King Ambarish, He sent forth the Sudarshan chakra. Kabirji says: such is my mighty Lord, who redeems the devotee who takes refuge in Him.

After this, Krupanath (the Gracious Lord) said to Durvasa: "Write out and show Me a thousand births." Then Durvasa, accordingly, wrote out a thousand births and showed them to Krupanath. At that, Krupanath erased one zero — and so nine hundred births were cut away. Then, seeing the Lord's love for His devotee, Durvasa himself struck off one more zero — and so another ninety births were removed. Then Krupanath, Shri Krishna, said: "Let us preserve the sage's dignity — even if he perceives this much, it is already a great deal — so, O King, the ten incarnations that now remain, you must bear."

At that moment, looking toward Durvasa, Ambarish spoke — and what did he say? Under the sway of the company of that sage, who is himself the embodiment of Time (kaal), Time had come to grip the King. Earlier, he had held a pure resolve, on account of which the Sudarshan chakra had withdrawn at the King's own word — but now that same feeling had faded away. The sage's shadow had fallen upon Ambarish, and that is why he spoke thus:

"O Maharaj! For Your own devotees there is no birth — that is what the scriptures say — so why then do You tell me that I must bear these ten incarnations?"

In this world, the glory of the company of good, saintly persons — of devotees of Hari — is very great, but if ever the company of a wicked person occurs, its bad effect does not fail to leave its mark. Of this, Durvasa now stands as a direct example. In this meeting, contact with the shadow of a wicked person brought a bad result. There are three examples of this. The first is this one of Durvasa. The second: when the sage Sanakadi and his brothers grew angry at Jaya and Vijaya, the fall of their shadow caused Jaya and Vijaya to accept devotion to the Lord through enmity instead. The third: when the shadow of the gods fell upon the gopis, the gopis became filled with pride, and because of that even the unbroken Ras-leela was broken. Also, the revered Yadunath Maharaj used to give a fourth example of the shadow of a wicked person, saying that in the body of a Patidar there is one bone that belongs to a demon (rakshasa), and because of it, when a bullock is goaded with the point of a driving-stick, he does not hesitate to jab it. It is said of the Patidars that they are the descendants of Sitaji's two sons, Lav and Kush — those descended from Lav became the Patidars called "Leva," and

those descended from Kush became the Patidars called "Kadva." These sons were born to Sitaji, upon whom the shadow of Ravan had fallen, and that is how demonic qualities entered the bodies of the Patidars. When Sitaji returned from Lanka to Ayodhya, the women of Ayodhya asked Sitaji what Ravan was like. Sitaji replied that she had never once looked directly at him, and so she did not know what he was like — but she had seen his big toe, and from that she had drawn a picture of what Ravan must have been like. This, then, is reckoned as the result of the shadow of a wicked person. In this way, the shadow of the wicked is the worst of all things, and it is for this very reason that saints and gurus advise us to keep the company of good people. Among us there is a saying:

_jaL dithe shuchi upaje. naari dithe kaam._
_kar kamaan kubuddhi upaje. maaLaa dithe raama._ ||19||

(On seeing water, the wish to bathe arises; on seeing a beautiful woman, desire for lust arises; when a bow comes into the hand, the urge to shoot an arrow awakens; on seeing a rosary, the wish to chant Ram's name arises.)

That is: on seeing water, the mind wishes to bathe; on seeing a beautiful woman, lustful desire is born; if a bow and arrow come into the hand, the wish to shoot the arrow awakens; on seeing a rosary, the mind wishes to chant the name of Ram.

Thus a shadow means that whatever a thing is, its effect is felt accordingly. Kabir has said:

_kabir deepak tha akela. tab niramal jyot prasavata._
_chhaya padi baatki. tab jaay pari khand khand._ ||20||

(When the lamp was alone, it spread a pure, unbroken light — but when the shadow of the intervening post fell across it, that light broke into pieces.)

When the lamp was alone, it used to spread a pure light, but when the shadow of the middle pillar fell across it and cast its shade, then that light became broken into fragments.

Even in the womb, if the child receives good impressions, that child grows up to be virtuous; but if the impressions of a wicked person fall upon it, that child is born unworthy. That is why pregnant women should read good scriptures and perform good bhajan — this is especially necessary. Here, we see that even a devotee like Ambarish had his understanding corrupted by the shadow of Durvasa. The influence of place and time, too, falls upon the human mind — and so it is only some rare, valiant, saintly person who can master themselves in such a situation. It is said that in Kurukshetra the demons were of such enormous size that when Kartikeya Swami slew Mahishasur and cut off his head, that severed head occupied a space of sixteen yojanas in Kurukshetra — and this is no exaggeration. Even our own shadow grows large in the morning and evening — but the point being made is that wherever the shadow of a wicked person has fallen, in that place — Kurukshetra — the very nature of people who go there turns wrathful; that is why Lord Krishna chose this very site of Kurukshetra for the Mahabharat war. Therefore everyone should walk carefully, wary of the wicked and evil-minded. It is for this very reason that Kabirji and Jivanji insist so strongly on staying far from the company of the wicked and the vile.

The same holds true for time as well. In the Kali Yuga, people begin to commit evil deeds; so if anyone at all escapes the influence of place and time, such a rare one can only be a saintly person — for no shadow of such place or time falls upon him. That is why, by remaining in the refuge of the Guru and the saints, we too can be saved from such shadows.

Hearing King Ambarish speak these words, Shri Krishna said: "O best among men! It is true, according to the scriptures, that there is no birth for Your own devotee — but it is likewise according to the scriptures that Durvasa's word must be kept. So I, for My part, must keep My devotee's word. Therefore, O best among men, in your place I shall Myself take on these ten incarnations." Having spoken these words, Shri Krishna fell silent, and the King remained listening.

How did this come to happen? While Ambarish was resolving Durvasa's crisis, and while this very exchange was taking place, the shadow of Durvasa was falling upon the King's toe. Because of this, Ambarish came under the sage's influence, and lost the discernment that Parbrahma should not be made to suffer trouble on his behalf. Jivanji Maharaj explains that when the shadow of a wicked person falls, even truth (sat) turns into untruth (asat). Thus, by the falling of Durvasa's shadow, a change came over Ambarish's mind, and the Lord was compelled to take birth in the mortal world and assume ten incarnations. Jivanji Maharaj says that without taking on a (human) birth, devotion to Vishnu cannot be practised, and that is why the saints have asked for human life instead of liberation. The devotee Narsinh Mehta, too, has sung of this:

_bhutaL bhakti padaarath moTun_
_brahma lokman naahi re._
_punya kari amaraapuri paamya,_
_ante choraashi maanhi re._ ||1||
_harina jan to mukti na maage,_
_maage janmo janma avataara re._
_nitya seva, nitya kirtan,_
_ochchhav nirakhavaa nandkumaar re._ ||2||

(The great treasure of devotion belongs to this earthly world — it is not to be found even in the realm of Brahma. Those who reach the immortal abode through their merit still, in the end, fall back into the cycle of eighty-four lakh births. The devotees of Hari do not ask for liberation — they ask instead for birth after birth after birth, so that they may forever have daily service, daily kirtan, and the joy of beholding the festivities of Nandkumar (Krishna).)

And again, in another pada further on, Narsinh Mehta says:

_praan thaki mune vaishnav vahaala, raat divas rude bhaaLu re._

(The Lord says: "Vaishnavs — that is, My devotees — are dearer to Me than My very life; day and night I hold them within My heart.")

The Lord says that Vaishnavs — that is, His devotees — are exceedingly dear to Him; that is why, setting aside His own pride, He took ten incarnations in Ambarish's place. Further —

_beTho gaay tahaan ubho re saambhaLun. ubho gaay tahaan naachun re._

(Wherever My devotee sits and sings, there I stand and listen; wherever he stands and sings, there I dance.)

Here Kabirji's sakhi says:

_kabir mansa janma durlabh hai. dehi na vaaryamvaarya._
_taravar (je) phal jhadpade. so bahorya na laage daarya._ ||25||

(Kabir says: human birth is very hard to attain; this body does not come again and again. Just as a fruit that falls from the tree can never again attach itself to the branch.)

Ambarish let slip this precious opportunity of such a fine human birth. In this sakhi, Kabirji says that human birth is very hard to obtain, that the human body does not come again and again — just as a fruit that falls from a tree can never again attach itself to the branch. In another sakhi, Kabirji speaks about the fruit and the tree:

_kabir bichhadanme dukh bohot hai. jaise phal aur daal._
_tahaanthe bichhadaa gir padaa. turat hi pakadaa kaal._ ||21||

Meaning: There is great sorrow in separation. Just as it is for the fruit and the branch — the moment it separates and falls, death seizes it at once. In the same way, one who separates from Ram meets this same fate.

In the Udadharma Panchratnamala, page 705-706, in Ashavari-7, the last verse-line is:

_durlabh dehi maanaviyaan keri. vaLi avani avataar re._
_kripaa karo tamo narasaiyaane. je gun tamaaraa gaaye re._ ||22||

(Human birth is exceedingly hard to attain, and taking birth again on this earth is likewise rare. Show grace, O Lord, upon this Narsaiya, who sings Your praises.)

In the Udadharma Panchratnamala, page 595, in Bhupal-2, it is said:

_tumhi gopaal mose bohot kari. tumhi dayaal mose bohot kari._
_sumaranakun nar dehi dini. mo paapi te kachhu na sarayo._

(You, O Gopal, have shown me great grace; You, O Merciful One, have shown me great grace — You gave this human body for remembrance and worship, but nothing of that work could be accomplished by a sinner such as I.)

You, O Lord, showed great grace upon me and gave me a human body, so that I could perform remembrance and kirtan — but from a sinner like me nothing of that work could be brought to completion. Khojiji says:

_phal Tuti jalmen padaa. khoji miti na pyaas._
_guru taji govind bhaje. taahi narak nivaas._ ||23||

(A fruit that breaks loose from the tree and falls into water — even then, says Khoji, its thirst is not quenched. One who abandons the Guru and worships Govind directly must dwell in hell.)

If a fruit breaks off from the tree and falls into water, it cannot be nourished by that water, nor can its thirst be quenched by it; likewise, one who abandons the Guru and directly performs devotion to the Lord must go to hell. Jivanji Maharaj has expressed the wish that the Lord should take on human incarnation age after age, in this mortal world:

_guru taruvar govind jal. sevak phal samaan._
_bhaav diT laagaa rahai. to nipaje niravaan._ ||24||

Meaning: The Guru is like a tree, the Lord — formless and unmanifest — is like water, and the devotee is like the fruit of that tree; but only if this fruit, which is the devotee, clings with loving devotion to the stalk of the Guru-tree — that is, to the Guru's own teaching — does it attain moksha, the highest good.

_guru vimukh jo hari bhaje. taakaa kaaj na hoy._
_unchaa chadhi neechaa gire. paai rad sab khoy._ ||25||

Meaning: If, having turned away from the Guru, one worships the Lord directly, one's task of crossing the ocean of worldly existence is not accomplished. Even though a fruit hangs upon the tree, if it forsakes the tree and falls down below, then all the comfort it received from the tree that nourished and sustained it is lost, and whatever high station it had attained becomes cancelled and useless. In the same way, though a disciple may, through the grace of the Guru, have attained a high station with the Lord, by turning away from the Guru he loses that high station and falls into a state of decline. Baba Kabir says:

_guru bin maalaa pherate. guru bin dete daan._
_guru bin sab nishphal gayaa. puchho ved puraan._ ||26||

Meaning: If one turns the rosary or gives charity without faith in the Guru's word, having turned away from the Guru, then all of this becomes useless without the Guru. Look into the Vedas and Puranas, and they too will give the same opinion. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says:

_aadhaa mataa saadhakaa. jahaan parabrahmaki aas._
_puraa mata tahaan jivanaa. jahaan sadguru shabd vishvaas._ ||27||

(Guru)

Meaning: Those who hold the opinion that one may cross over by devotion to the Lord without a Guru hold a view that is not wholly true — it is only half true. But those who understand that devotion must be practised with faith in the teaching of the Sadguru — their view is entirely correct.

_aadhaa mata kon kaamkaa. je paave vaikunthko dhaam._
_taathe jagat bhalo jivanaa. kabahu sant sangat vishraam._ ||28||

(Sant)

Meaning: Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says that those who, by worshipping the family deity and such minor deities, attain heaven or Vaikuntha, still attain only a half, incomplete abode — so of what use is such a view, held with such expectation, in worshipping a lesser deity? It is better to remain in this world, so that once in a while one may have the good fortune to revel in the company of saints. Therefore the intention (view) of attaining heaven and such through ritual and obligatory religious acts is incomplete. Jivanji Maharaj says:

_pitaa hamaaraa raamji. maataa satavanti naar._
_jug jug maagun jivanaa. ghare maanav avataar._ ||29||

Meaning: Human life is exceedingly rare, and it is in this very birth that the soul obtains the golden opportunity to attain the Lord. In all other births, the soul must simply undergo the fruits of its past deeds, whereas this present opportunity is unique — for in it the soul, casting off its own ignorance, becomes aware enough to recognize Parbrahma. Thus, on obtaining a human birth, the soul comes to discern the truth of all its identities, and experiences the sorrow of having become separated from that from which it came — that is, from Parbrahma — and can become resolutely determined to free itself from the cycle of birth and death and become one with Parbrahma. "Therefore, O Lord, take a human incarnation and grant us our well-being." Adhyaruji Maharaj, showing the way to be freed from this, states:

_junaa bhogavi niragame navaa taNo kare parihaar._
_eNi pere nishkarma jo hoy to havadaa hoy paar._ ||6||

Thus Adhyaruji Maharaj shows us the direct and simple way to gain freedom from this whirlwind of karma: exhaust and finish off the old deeds by undergoing their fruits, and give up new ones — that is, one should not perform new deeds. In this way, freed of karma, the soul can attain Parbrahma. But if, having come into this world, one falls under the sway of maya, then instead of giving up new deeds one goes on adding to them, and once again the cycle of birth and death starts up anew.

_kim karma kim karmeti kavayo'pyatra mohitaah._
_tatte karma pravakshyaami yajjnaatvaa mokshyase'shubhaat._ ||16||

(Gita 4.16)

"What is action, and what is inaction?" — even the wise are confused on this matter. Therefore I shall explain to you both action and inaction, knowing which you shall be freed from inauspicious bondage.

For this reason Adhyaruji Maharaj says:

_vaN hari bhakti ajaaNave. na lahe koi taaro maram._
_krit karma bhogave ek game. biji game saache karam._

"Ek game" means undergoing the old deeds on one side, and "biji game" means adding new deeds on the other side. But if one takes refuge in the name of the Lord, one gains the state of freedom from action (nishkarma).

Thus, if instead of giving up karma one goes on performing more karma, then this most precious human birth, once obtained, goes to waste. Today the world has become so given over to materialism that Adhyaruji Maharaj speaks the plain truth indeed: on one side one undergoes the fruits of past deeds, and on the other side one keeps accumulating new deeds. Thus, watching one and forgetting the other, in this deceptive creation the soul comes to relish deeds themselves; and then, without effort, it turns that way and keeps forgetting its own true duty. In this world, in such a whirlwind of deeds, even the greatest of the great lose their way. In this maze of confusion, King Ambarish too has lost his way, and he came to raise the question: "How can a devotee of Vishnu even have a birth?" To understand karma is an exceedingly difficult task. How to keep the soul free from karma while living in the world, taking part in all its worldly rites and activities, remains a knotty question — and even many learned scholars have no answer to it. But Jivanji Maharaj has made it easy for us to give up karma, and has shown us the way of freedom from action. Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai, Namdev, Karmabai, Rohidas, and others have walked this path. Yet here, even the supreme devotee Ambarish lost his way. Adhyaruji Maharaj says:

_hari ye amareesh narapati chhetaryo e, joge avataryo e. swamiji dashe avataar._

Adhyaruji Maharaj says that the King was deceived and remained caught in a false notion, and thereby missed his most precious opportunity. In the King's place, the Lord gave His word to take ten incarnations. Instead of the devotee, it was the Lord who had to bear the hardship. This, then, was the shortfall that came into Ambarish's devotion. A devotee should always remain ready to serve the Lord — but instead, it was the Lord who was made to bear hardship. (In the Samagam, Jivanji Maharaj cites this word in Vidurji's name, saying it comes from Bhagwat 9-5-12 to 16 — that word is actually Durvasa's and Shukdev's. It shows how much humility is called for, not only for the Lord, but for His devotee as well.)

The 27th shlok here is actually the 21st of the Pandav-gita, and it is Virat's own word — so, in place of Vidur, it should be understood as Virat's statement. According to the terms agreed upon in the Mahabharat, the Pandavas were to remain in hiding for one year without being discovered, and for this they chose the city of Virat. At the end of the year, when the Pandavas were recognized, King Virat felt great sorrow over one thing: that devotees as dear to the Lord as the Pandavas had lived in his house as servants! So he prayed and asked the Lord for this one single boon:

_vaasudevasya ye bhaktaah shaantaastyaktamaanasah._
_teshaam daasasya daaso'ham bhaveyam janmani janmani._ ||27||

(Whoever are the devotees of Vasudev, whose minds too rest in Him — of their devotees I shall become the servant of their servant, in every birth in this world.)

(This commentary belongs to the shlokas of Bhagwat Skandha 9-5-12 to 16.)

That is: what are the true devotees of Vasudevji like? They are people of great intelligence. Devotees of Vishnu are of far-reaching wisdom; they possess discernment, for they know good from bad. Moreover, they walk the path of devotion with discretion. They are, further, of great spiritual advancement. They wish to know nothing other than devotion to Vishnu. And they are so humble and discerning that they are ready to become the servant even of the devotee's servant — and that not for one birth alone, but for birth after birth. If that is so, then why did Ambarish's mind change? Why did he refuse to take birth? Such questions arise — what, then, is the answer to these questions?

Durvasa was standing before the King's very sight, and it was the falling of his shadow that caused Ambarish's mind to change — and the Lord then made ready to take incarnation, and took on ten incarnations. Jivanji Maharaj says that whatever the wishes of a devotee, such is his Protector. The King's own wishes changed, and so the Lord fulfilled those changed wishes and took ten incarnations. What were these ten incarnations? Jaydevji has sung of them:

_vedaanuddharate jaganti vahate bhugolamudbibhrate._
_daityam daarayate balim chhalayate kshatrakshayam kurvate._
_paulastyam jayate halam kalayate kaarunyamaatanvate._
_mlechchhaan murchhayate dashaakritikrite krishnaaya tubhyam namah._ ||28||

(Geet Govind 1-2-1)

(To You, O Krishna, who redeemed the Vedas [Matsya], who bore the worlds [Kurma], who upheld the sphere of the earth [Varaha], who tore apart the demon [Narasimha], who deceived Bali [Vamana], who brought about the destruction of the kshatriyas [Parashuram], who conquered Ravan, son of Pulastya [Ram], who bears the plough [Balaram], who spreads compassion [Buddha], and who will bewilder the mlecchhas [Kalki] — You who took these ten forms — to You, my salutations.)

Commentary: In the form of Matsya, He redeemed the Vedas and gave them to Brahma. According to the story in the Matsya Purana, in the seventh Manvantar divine teaching was given to the seventh Manu, Vaivasvat, and to the Saptarshis. Also, at the time of the deluge, a demon named Hayagriva stole away the Vedas and other scriptures and fled into the netherworld; then, taking the form of Matsya, the Lord redeemed the Vedas and the rest. Thus, for the welfare of all, Parbrahma came, and made Ambarish His pretext for doing so. In the second incarnation He appeared in the form of Kurma, and the fourteen jewels were obtained; of these, He Himself married Lakshmiji, wore the Kaustubh gem upon His chest, and distributed the remaining jewels among the other gods. In all of this, what task of King Ambarish's own was accomplished? In the third incarnation, in the form of Varaha, He slew Hiranyaksha, and He Himself wedded the Earth, and entrusted Brahma with the work of creation and so on. In this incarnation too, He carried out the protection of creation in Ambarish's name. In the fourth incarnation, in the form of Narasimha, He killed Hiranyakashipu and redeemed Prahlad. In the fifth incarnation, in the form of Vamana, He granted King Bali an unshakeable kingdom in the netherworld, and protected Indra's own throne. In the sixth incarnation He appeared as Parashuram and made the earth free of kshatriyas. In the seventh incarnation He appeared as Ram and slew Ravan, and put an end to the deeds of Kumbhakarna. In the eighth incarnation, in the form of Balram-Balabhadra, He bore the plough and destroyed the mlecchhas and the like. In the ninth incarnation, appearing as Buddha, He practised meditation and redeemed countless beings. In the tenth incarnation, as Kalki, He will destroy the yavanas and the like.

All these ten incarnations He Himself took on, in King Ambarish's place. What task of Ambarish's own was accomplished through all these incarnations? Did any fruit come to him from it? Neither was devotion to Vishnu practised through it, nor was any work for the welfare of the people accomplished through it. Whatever was done, the Lord Himself did it — that is, King Ambarish was deceived, and it was the Lord who had to take incarnation in his place. In this, the King himself remained free of action, and yet became burdened with the fault of action. And whose word, after all, was kept — Durvasa's? If we look at it plainly, King Ambarish did clearly refuse. The Lord gave assurance that He would keep His word — but Jivanji Maharaj explains that the Lord goes wherever there is the wish of the devotee, and takes whatever form suits whatever need arises for whoever is in distress. The Lord has been called bhakt-vatsal — ever tender toward His devotees. He is always present to protect His own devotees. Here, the Lord kept the word of both — of Durvasa and of Ambarish — and in doing so, deceived them both.

_bhakt manorath jivanaa. hari ghare dase avataar._
_nrip rishi dou chhetare. prabhu leela anant apaar._ ||27||

(Dasaka Ang – 59)

In this way, the Lord comes at a single call for help — and foremost among these are Ram and Krishna. The Lord's Leela, moreover, is unbroken. Through His incarnations the Lord has accomplished many tasks. What, then, is meant by His taking ten incarnations? These are simply the names given to His various forms. The Leela that belongs to Ram and to Krishna — these are, after all, only the names of the One who holds the Leela. In assuming this form, whose name was taken, and for what reason?

Wherever, and whatever distress a devotee faces, there the Lord has assumed a corresponding form. Wherever there is a particular form, there a corresponding name too has been given.

That is: there is no end to the Lord's Leela. Moreover, the various Puranic tales are also full of the Lord's incarnations, deeds, the relationships between gods and demons, and the relationships among the Lord's various gods and goddesses, vow-stories, the glories of pilgrimage sites, and so on. In such Puranic tales an ordinary person may often become confused; it also happens that many Puranic stories contradict one another. At such times it becomes exceedingly difficult to find and know the truth. So then, what is this matter of the ten incarnations spoken of here? The answer to that will be given further on.

Here, once again, the word of the all-pervading Leela:

_dhanpat swaroopi raam hai. laheri ve avataar._
_aage pichhe madhyas jal. taakaa e vistaar._ ||28||

Meaning: That Parbrahma-Parmatma who came to Ambarish's aid plays out many roles, as an actor (a performer of plays) does, and in this way He has played the roles of the ten incarnations and so on. But all the people of the world, seeing such various incarnations, keep taking the Lord to be many different beings in many different ways — yet this Lord is not really different from Himself; it is one and the same Lord who, like an actor, assumes different forms.

He who plays throughout all things is Parbrahma in the form of Ram — that is the master of "dhan" (rain-wealth), the ocean; and the waves are the ten incarnations. Before, behind, and in the middle of the waves is the water in the form of Brahma-consciousness — that is its extent. In the incarnation that came before, the one in the middle, and the one that will come after — in each, that same Parbrahma in the form of Ram alone abides.

Parbrahma is like the ocean; the ten incarnations are its waves. The water at the very centre of this ocean is in the form of Ram-Krishna — this is called Naam-roop (name as form). And what comes before and after — that is, the ten incarnations that come before and after Ram-Krishna — these are called Roop-naam (form as name). Further, at the time of the Ras-leela, there was one Krishna between each and every gopi — this was because, of the gopis who had adorned themselves with the sixteen ornaments, each one, like a mirror, reflected the form of Krishna in many different ways. But the original form of Krishna was that one true Krishna around whose neck Radhaji had placed her arms while performing the Ras-leela — that alone was the real Krishna. The rest — the Krishnas seen reflected in the gopis' adornments — were, like reflections in a mirror, mere appearances only. And the Lord who came to Ambarish's aid was this very same original Parbrahma-Parmatma. So the Krishna seen in such adornment-like reflections could not have given such help, because that is only an appearance (aabhaas) of Parbrahma; and since the ten incarnations, too, are of this same nature — mere appearances of the Lord — they are counted and reckoned only as names given to that form, names attached to the form of the incarnation, resembling the Krishna seen in the gopis' adornments — from these, it is useless to expect any real help.

The water in the midst of Radhaji's hands is the flute-charming Krishna — that is the very form of the Supreme Being. He alone is the doer and sustainer of the world. The Lord is formless (nirgun, niraakaar), and that is why He has been compared to water. Radhaji's hand rests around the neck of this very Lord Krishna, and that is why Radhaji is able to relish the joy of this Leela of the Lord. But when the shadow of the gods fell, the Lord became invisible — yet He went away taking Radhaji along with Him. That is why it is said, on page 77 of the Samagam, that Radhaji had become filled with pride — Radhaji felt that "the Lord is in the midst of my very hands" — and so the Lord, taking Radha along, became invisible. That is, it points us toward the truth that one should be free of pride — for even when Radhaji herself became proud, the Lord departed even from her presence.

Now, what is meant by this "water in the midst of Radhaji's hands"? For this, two kinds of statement have been made — Naam-roop and Roop-naam. In place of Ambarish, the Lord agreed to take ten incarnations; in those incarnations, whatever form the Lord assumed, a name accordingly arose — but that was not the Lord's original, permanent form; so in that incarnation, whatever form the Lord had, that very same was its name — hence that is "Roop-naam." But the Lord who assumes such incarnations — that original Parbrahma is called "Naam-roop." Hence that alone is the true Supreme Being of Naam-roop. In the palm of a hand, water can remain only in a very tiny quantity. On this there is a riddle:

"A shallow pond, a shallow bank — not even a paisa's worth of water stays" — the answer to which is: a palm. In a palm, only a negligible amount of water can remain — so in Radhaji's hands is the formless (nirgun) Krishna, who is not like such a shallow pond, but is of Naam-roop; so in this pond that is of Roop-naam, there is only the mere appearance of the formless Parbrahma. In the Bhagwat it is said:

_avataaraa hyasankhyeyaa hareh sattvanidhervijaah._
_yathaa'vinaashinah kulyaah sarasah syuh sahasrashah._ ||17||

(9-3-26)

(O Brahmins! Just as thousands of small, unfailing streams flow out from an inexhaustible lake, in that same way countless incarnations arise from Shri Hari, the ocean of the quality of sattva.)

O Brahmins! Just as thousands of little rivers flow out from an inexhaustible lake, in the same way countless incarnations arise from Shri Hari, the ocean of the quality of sattva.

Just as there is a cycle of transformation in the oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen cycles, so too a cycle of transformation runs its course here.

That is: "dhan" — meaning clouds and rain — has as its lord the ocean; from the ocean's own water, vapour forms and becomes clouds of wealth-rain, and these same clouds come back down again in the form of rain, and the water returns once more to the ocean. This process goes on continually. The tales told of the Ocean of Milk in the Puranas and other scriptures are of this very same kind — a Leela of Parbrahma — in which creation arises, and in the end is again absorbed back into that very same source. Whatever substance, thing, or object — moving or unmoving — exists in this world, all of it is but the various forms of that same complete Parbrahma. But these forms are not unchanging — form is subject to breaking; form keeps changing. Whereas the name is unchanging, and imperishable. But when we utter a name, the very first thing that appears before our sight is a vision of its form. For instance, if someone utters the word "snake," before our very eyes there appears a fearsome, long, rope-like creature — even though it may not actually be physically present. No form need be physically present — but on hearing the name, its form becomes vividly present before us, indirectly. The illustration that was discussed at the very start of this chapter is here explained once again, with a fitting example: from the middle part of the ocean a wave arises, and dashes against the rocks of the shore. This wave is the incarnation. The wave is momentary. On the ocean's water, by the force of the wind, a wave arises; but only as long as the wind's control persists over it does its life continue — after that it is destroyed, and again a new wave comes. This process goes on unceasingly. In this, we can give a name to each and every wave. Each and every wave that arises completes its own lifespan and is destroyed. But if it is given a definite name, that name is not destroyed along with it, nor will it ever be. Names remain preserved for endless time. If we try once more to understand this metaphor: the entire ocean, in its one single body, is spread out everywhere, and its water, too, remains the very same — there is no increase or decrease in it, no change occurs in it. Even for the forming of clouds, the ocean's water goes up into the sky, and yet no decrease is seen in its quantity because of that, nor any increase from the coming of the rains; nor is any change seen in the ocean becoming saltier or less salty.

That is: in this world, in this universe, whatever things — moving and unmoving — are visible, and the countless multitudes of stars — in these too, increase and decrease go on occurring. Just as, in the ocean, sometimes more waves come and sometimes fewer, without that causing any real change — in exactly the same way, in this universe too, what is visible today may perhaps not be visible tomorrow; changes keep occurring in form — one comes while another goes. In just the same way, this is the arithmetic that governs Parbrahma's incarnations as well. Just as the wave that arises in the middle of the ocean — the name given to such waves is Ram and Krishna. Form undergoes destruction, but the name is never destroyed. The name is unchanging and imperishable; moreover, no defect or alteration ever occurs in it.

Once a name has been given, it does not change; the form changes — just as we give a name to a small child, but that child's form keeps changing with time. The one who was a small child becomes a grown boy, then a young man, becomes middle-aged too, and at last becomes a frail old person and finally passes away. Yet through every one of these stages, the name does not change.

Thus, what we call Ram and Krishna are names of the Form — and the ten incarnations spoken of, that came before and after, are likewise names of that same form. Further — what should this Form and this Name be called?

Here Jivanji Maharaj has posed a very deep and knotty question. Just as, in the Ras-leela, there was one Krishna between each and every sakhi (gopi) — that is, if a young woman, adorned and ready in her gleaming sixteen ornaments, were to be set with countless tiny mirrors, then as many reflections of whoever stood facing her would appear in them. Though the young woman is one, countless reflections of her appear all around her. In just the same way, in the Ras-leela, Radhaji is Prakriti (Nature itself), and the other gopis are but various forms of that very same Prakriti. Krishna has joined Himself, in various ways, with these various forms — that is, He is united with every form of Prakriti. But to see His reflection, a mirror is needed. This mirror is Radhaji, who is the subtle form of Prakriti. Shri Krishna and Radhaji cannot be seen in their gross, physical form, for to do so would serve no purpose.

"The water in the middle — that is the flute-charming Shri Krishna, in the midst of Radhaji's hands. This is His name — He who came to Ambarish's call! By Name-and-Form, He is truly this very flute-charming Supreme Lord; and by Form-and-Name — for what reason does that come about? What fruit is produced by worshipping that? This world, this universe, is a bond, a binding factor — it is bound by this very universe. Why should one be bound by it?"

That is: this is a Samagam saying. The all-powerful Parbrahma alone is the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. In the midst of Radhaji's hands is water — that is, the subtle form of water is the very cause by which Parbrahma becomes perceptible. It is from this subtle element of water that we are able to obtain outward knowledge — form, taste, smell, and so on. At the front surface of the pupil of the eye there is a moist film of water, by which sight is possible; there is water upon the tongue, and that is why we can experience taste. Thus every element of Nature has two aspects — one its gross form, and the other its subtle form. Parbrahma dwells, in subtle form, within every element — but this Parbrahma is not something that can be perceived by the senses; He is beyond the organs of action and of knowledge.
